"Disco Elysium" is more than a video game; it is a form of art that changes the way you see politics. In real life, you can say whatever nonsense you want, and nothing happens, but here, every decision you make has consequences. It's like having a philosophical debate in a bar, except instead of discussing, you end up kicking inanimate objects, and you feel like a damn monster for doing so.

It not only offers a fascinating universe filled with multiple plots and charismatic characters, but it also transforms how we see the consequences of our ideas. If reading a book is anything like this, I should definitely give it a try.

Playing Disco Elysium is just like studying thermodynamics. At first, you believe it's just about numbers - you think you can easily solve the most intricate crime or problem by merely playing the right hand. Then you see the big picture, and the interconnections between delicate systems capture you like a spider web. You begin wondering what kind of wicked god creates such a beautiful abomination. In the end, you give up finding the true essence as it is an infinite matryoshka doll. You know how to do the job, but its alluring magic haunts you forever.

I first picked this up on PS5 and thought it was incredible, but honestly? Replaying it on PC has been a total trip. I thought I’d seen everything Martinaise had to offer, but I was so wrong. I’m still stumbling into weird secrets and dialogue paths that I completely blew past the first time. The art style is just gorgeous it’s like walking through a living, breathing oil painting that’s slightly falling apart at the seams. But it’s the writing that really gets me. This time around, I’ve been catching all these soul-crushing, sad lines mixed with weirdly motivational stuff that actually hits home. It’s one of the few games that makes me stop and just stare at the screen for a minute because a line of dialogue called me out. I have to mention meeting the Insulindian Phasmid actually broke me. Between that music which felt so sad yet hopeful and the way it spoke, I was a total emotional mess. It felt like Harry was finally getting another chance to be happy, or at least a reason to keep going. Seeing Kim witness it with me just made the whole moment feel even more real. I’ve put so many hours into this and I’m still seeing stuff I’ve never seen before. My Inland Empire is probably working overtime, but I don't care. If you haven't played this yet, just do it. It’s a masterpiece.

This game is essentially interactive fiction, a choose-your-own-adventure book with isometric graphics reminiscent of old-school PC RPGs. There are puzzle-like situations to work through, but they are not like the adventure games of old; you will explore your environment, packrat away various useful-seeming items, and interact with NPCs via elaborate dialogue trees, but if you find yourself stuck, it won't be because you can't figure out what verb to use or which of your inventory items need to be nonsensically combined in order to progress. Any time my progress in Disco Elysium was stymied it was either because I needed to explore a new area of the map...or make some kind of decision that I'd been putting off. The skill system is unique and oriented toward creating narrative rather than blocking your way forward; failure can be as entertaining as success, and a great deal of the game's humor comes from the degree to which the protagonist is an absolute human disaster.

You will do a lot of reading, but it's interactive enough that it feels very different from simply picking up a novel. The characters are interesting and brought to life by just enough voice acting to establish them in your mind. The music and sounds add considerably to the game's atmosphere. The setting is intriguing and it would be great to see it explored further.

Also, you can die from sitting in a chair.

Disco Elysium is very definitely the best-written video game I've ever played. I cannot exaggerate the impressiveness and the depth of the storyline, characters and setting that make up this incredible title. It is a benchmark for excellence as far as world-building is concerned, and the agency it affords the player in sculpting the protagonist is extremely refreshing.

An extremely-dialogue driven RPG set in the fictional city of Revachol, Disco Elysium sees you as a disgraced police detective seemingly arousing from the worst day of his life. With no memory of his identity, no recollection of his mission, and no context to the world around him, it is up to the player to decide who this man is and what he will become as he attempts to solve a murder in a lawless ghetto besieged by imminent class war.

Every single question could have consequence, every action can concern a potential ally. Submit to every vice around you and stumble through the case as a broken detective spiralling into madness, or go cold-turkey and turn this mystery around as a super-cop rising from the ashes of your old life like a phoenix? The choice is entirely yours, and in a truly welcome rarity, that's actually the truth.
